text: Charts hold the numbers that matter, in news, textbooks and reports. But to a screen reader, a chart is just a picture. Ask what this one says, and you get one word.
Blind and low-vision readers lose the data. And many sighted people struggle with charts too.
This is ChartVoice. It lets anyone hear, read and check the real numbers inside a chart image.
Let's give it that same chart. An image AI model reads the data straight from the pixels. Online, that's a Groq vision model. Offline, Google's DePlot runs on your laptop.
First, the answer in plain words, with the highest, the lowest and the trend as big numbers. One click reads it aloud, and highlights each sentence.
You can also hear the shape of the chart. Higher values play higher notes.
Or move point by point with the arrow keys. Each point is announced.
Still curious? Ask a question in plain words. The answer comes from your chart's numbers.
Here's how it works. The image AI turns the picture into a data table. That's the heart of the project. Without it, there are no numbers.

Then our own code computes the facts: highest, lowest, trend, biggest change. Plain arithmetic, never guessed. A language model only writes the sentences, and every number it uses is checked against the table.
AI can still misread a chart, so ChartVoice lets you check its work. A sighted helper can compare your image with a chart redrawn from the numbers.
Every number is in a real table, ready to download. And you can see what a generic AI says, side by side.
We measured it. On eleven charts we generated with known data, the offline reader got sixty-five of sixty-seven values within five percent, and the highest value every time.
And it's built for access from the start: keyboard first, screen reader announcements, high contrast, and text that scales up.
Next, we want PDFs, more chart types, and a browser extension. ChartVoice. Hear, read and check the numbers inside any chart.
